Ahead of Trump-Xi meetings, US presses China on trade pledges

"I emphasized the importance of China fully and immediately honouring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a social media post.

WASHINGTON: The Trump administration warned a top Chinese official on Friday (Nov 6) that Beijing must immediately implement its commitments under a nearly year-old trade agreement, particularly on delivery of rare earths and other critical minerals and agricultural purchases, the United States Trade Representative's Office said. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer urged Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in a call to implement terms of the pact agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, the US agencies said. "During the call, Ambassador Greer emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths and other critical minerals," USTR said in a statement. During the call, China expressed "serious concern" over recent US trade restrictions targeting Beijing, China's official Xinhua news agency said.

But He, China's lead negotiator on trade relations with the US, agreed with his US counterparts to continue using consultation for "stable and positive" development of trade ties, Xinhua reported. Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, on Nov 18 and 19, and the Group of 20 summit in Miami on Dec 14 and 15. Greer said the Trump administration will pursue balanced trade with China by "monitoring compliance of past commitments while unlocking lasting benefits for American farmers, ranchers, manufacturers, and workers". Greer, Bessent and other US officials have frequently complained about difficulties that US companies say they are experiencing in receiving sufficient quantities of rare earths and other critical minerals from China under the Busan agreement. The US says the deal was designed to lift restrictions put in place in 2025 during a period of tariff escalations between the world's two largest economies. The Busan trade deal, which expires on Jan 10, capped US tariffs on Chinese goods implemented during Trump's second term at about 20 per cent. China has pledged to buy 25 million metric tons of US soybeans for the next three years and boost purchases of other American farm goods by US$17 billion. "I emphasized the importance of China fully and immediately honouring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results," Bessent said in a social media post. The US will "closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement", the Treasury said in a statement. Beijing has signaled tariff concessions remain central to its aims, with its commerce ministry saying on Thursday that China was open to buying more US farm goods, but only if the two sides implement their reciprocal tariff-cut agreement. Following a September summit between Xi and Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has not been finalised. The White House said in May that Beijing had agreed to buy US$17 billion of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year's target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made in October last year to buy US soybeans.

Source: Reuters/cf

Paraguay president ousted and placed under house arrest, successor sworn in

Santiago Peña was ousted from the presidency about an hour beforehand in a unanimous Senate vote, with lawmakers citing questions over his past links to the collapsed digital bank ueno that had provided accounts for nearly half of Paraguay's population.

ASUNCION, Paraguay: Pedro Alliana was sworn in as Paraguay's new president on Friday (Nov 6) just as authorities put his impeached predecessor Santiago Peña under house arrest, the latest developments in a fast-moving political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of a digital bank. Prosecutors speaking outside Peña's house in Asunción said charges were still being determined but could include influence peddling. Peña was ordered to appear at the prosecutor's office on Saturday morning.

Paraguay's Vice President Pedro Alliana is sworn in after President Santiago Pena was removed from office in an impeachment trial, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Nov 6, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Cesar Olmedo)

Peña was ousted from the presidency about an hour beforehand in a unanimous Senate vote, with lawmakers citing questions over his past links to the collapsed digital bank ueno that had provided accounts for nearly half of Paraguay's population. Although Peña offered his resignation on Thursday, the Senate chose to finalise the impeachment process rather than accept, and swiftly moved to install his second-in-command, Alliana.

By the time of his arrest, dozens of protesters had gathered outside Peña's residence. Police installed a security cordon around the property. The turmoil began earlier this week when Paraguay's central bank intervened in ueno, whose customers include many people who had not previously had access to a bank account. The bank had grown rapidly since launching in 2021. But questions had emerged over ueno's lending practices and its ties to Paraguay's political and financial elite - including Peña, who until last year was a shareholder in ueno's holding company, and the central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, who had headed ueno until 2023. Prosecutors on Friday also issued an arrest warrant for Carvallo, who resigned earlier this week as authorities launched last-ditch proceedings to prevent the lender dissolving. Eight former ueno executives have already been detained. Others from Peña's inner circle also resigned, including his interior minister, chief of staff and two advisers. The impeachment charges that led to his removal alleged that Peña had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña denied any wrongdoing and said the affair was a regulatory issue. The central bank has denied any conflict of interest, saying Carvallo recused himself from all decisions related to ueno. FROZEN ACCESS TO FUNDS The political crisis has spilled onto the streets, with demonstrators flocking to downtown Asuncion demanding accountability for ueno's collapse and faster compensation for depositors whose savings remain frozen. Small groups of protesters gathered opposite the headquarters of the central bank on Friday, chanting "We want our money."

People protest outside Congress during a session to discuss President Santiago Pena's resignation, days after Paraguay's central bank took over Ueno Bank amid a solvency crisis, in Asuncion, Paraguay, Thursday, Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: AP/Jorge Saenz)

Those who have been unable to access their accounts include pensioners who receive state benefits through ueno. Peña earlier this week approved legislation to help accelerate payments to affected depositors and some account holders began recovering their money on Thursday. Prospects for a lengthy political transition have drawn attention from investors, especially in neighboring Brazil, Paraguay's largest economic partner. Regulators have sought to reassure markets by guaranteeing most deposits and containing risks to the wider financial system. A Brazilian government source told Reuters that Brazil's immediate concern was avoiding social instability in Paraguay and ensuring the banking crisis is resolved without triggering wider unrest. "Protests over frozen savings will intensify if Peña's exit appears to grant him impunity or if payouts to depositors and pensioners stall," said Mariano Machado, Americas principal analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

Source: Reuters/cf

Newsroom bomb threats follow escalating European flight hoaxes

The messages, headlined "Message to the West", portrayed the threats as a prelude to attacks on means of transport across Europe.

BUDAPEST/DUBLIN/PRAGUE: Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov", claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe. The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.  The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat. Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails, or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

But they added to concern among European officials that the hoaxes are part of a campaign of "hybrid" disruptions, which many have blamed on Russia, aimed at countries that have helped Ukraine. Moscow has denied involvement. Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare". No explosive devices were found, and all planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.

Related:

Fighter jet escorts, flight diversions: What we know about Europe’s wave of hoax bomb threats

FLIGHT DISRUPTIONS LESSEN Security experts said on Thursday that the threats might be intended to punish European nations that have armed or financed Ukraine as it resists the full-scale invasion Russia launched in 2022. It was also possible, however, that individuals were laying false trails, issuing copycat threats or acting on personal grievances. Around half a dozen flights were disrupted in some way on Tuesday and more than two dozen on Thursday, some of them making unplanned landings or being escorted to their destinations by fighter jets. On Friday, an Italian airport authority source said a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome had been diverted to Venice but, despite more than a dozen hoax threats, overall there was far less direct disruption to air travel. Hungarian jets did, however, escort airliners flying from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Bucharest and Cyprus through Hungarian airspace. Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said NATO had ordered some air patrols in the area, the first report that the Western defence alliance had become involved. While no country attributed blame for the threats, they follow a wave of sabotage attacks and attempts on targets across Europe ranging from German electricity substations to defence-related facilities in the Baltic region, and supermarket refrigerators in France and elsewhere. Germany blamed Russia directly for a drone attack on Leipzig airport.

Related:

Fridge cyberattack hits supermarkets across Europe

French blood banks hit alongside cyberattack on European supermarkets

EU COMMISSIONER SAYS RUSSIA IS OFTEN TO BLAME FOR ATTACKS Many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response. European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen told Reuters on Thursday that since 2022 Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference. “We are under attack all the time,” she said. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilise our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.” “It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations," she said, adding: "Quite often it is Russia.” On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State", a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia. Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.

Source: Reuters/fs

Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday (Nov 6), after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. The announcement comes at the end of a bruising week for Musk as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in Tuesday's US midterm elections , with the vast majority of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races. Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than US$370 billion in market capitalisation for the week.

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialised components for the heavy, angular model. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era". Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US electric vehicle maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024. Around the start of production in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth US$131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

Related:

Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing

US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test

"CYBERTRUCK WON'T GO, CAN'T GO" Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future". But the model has struggled to meet those expectations. Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates. Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pickups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pickups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. MUSK'S NEW BET The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X. However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon. The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year. Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units. About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles.

Source: Reuters/dc

WASHINGTON: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a video message on Thursday (Nov 5) vowing to fight efforts in Congress to impeach him and defending the Iran war as “courageous and historic” after voters punished Republicans over it in this week’s midterm elections . Hegseth's remarks, posted on social media, came as taunts from his foes in Congress intensified and President Donald Trump swatted away questions about whether he might fire Hegseth . Trump has commended his Pentagon chief. The top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, asked in a post: "Why is Pete Hegseth still around?" Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has been a polarising figure who has made enemies even within his own Republican Party. Critics in Congress are targeting his conduct of the Iran war, which Vice President JD Vance has said cost Republicans control of Congress, his firing of top military officers and strained relations with lawmakers as the administration seeks a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package. Democrats, who won control of Congress in Tuesday's elections, have promised to investigate Hegseth and his handling of the Pentagon, and congressional aides say that would include the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, among other issues. Republican Representative Thomas Massie promised to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth next week, warning that impeachment would be "much gentler" than what's in store for him once Republicans cede control of Congress next year to Democrats. "They’ll have hearings & trials," Massie wrote on X. Hegseth defended his stewardship of the Pentagon in a more than four-minute video that boasted about firing senior Pentagon leaders, ending diversity initiatives and banning transgender individuals from the military. "You see, they attack me - they attack us - because we are effective. It's not going to work. We will not back down," Hegseth said to the camera. Calling the impeachment effort a "sham," Hegseth said that Trump himself was impeached twice. "It's all about the politics of personal destruction. It didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me. You can rest assured of that," he said. Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth when asked whether he expected any staffing changes, saying his defence secretary had "done a fantastic job" and suggesting that the opposition to him was tied to his firing of generals. "We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it. And many of those people were woke. I don't like a woke general. And so, he probably has opposition," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. Trump also praised Hegseth's role in US military operations in Venezuela and Iran. "Venezuela has been unbelievable ... and in Iran, we are there for seven months and we control everything that we've wanted to control," he said.

Related:

Republicans call for Trump to change course after midterm drubbing

Trump says Hegseth doing 'a very good job' as questions swirl about his future

CHOPPING BLOCK Sources have said Trump could still replace Hegseth as Republicans assess their election losses. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance publicly questioned whether the Iran war was worth it and said it cost Republicans control of Congress, in extraordinary remarks that raised questions about whether Trump might still go ahead with a threatened resumption of major combat operations against Iran. One Trump adviser said Hegseth "could be on the chopping block" because of the Iran war. The Defense Department has said Hegseth is "100 per cent committed" to leading the Pentagon until the end of Trump's term. Hegseth appealed to "patriotic" lawmakers to pass a funding request that aims to help the Pentagon pay for the Iran war and other spending priorities. "Regardless of how people feel about the war, which I believe is a courageous and historic effort that will ensure Iran never gets nuclear weapons, we need to continue, as President Trump did in his first term, to rebuild our military," Hegseth said. Republican US Senator Thom Tillis told CBS on Tuesday night that Hegseth has "a reckoning" coming and his strained relationship with lawmakers was undermining the Trump administration's push for a US$1.5 trillion defence spending package in Congress. Hegseth could also face scrutiny from Democrats over his Ukraine policy and US military strikes on suspected drug trafficking boats in Latin American waters, which some Democrats say could amount to war crimes. Representative Adam Smith, the Democrat who is expected to lead the House Armed Services Committee next year, promised vigorous oversight on everything from the Iran war to what he called the erosion of the "apolitical foundation of the armed forces".

Source: Reuters/nh
